content: In the field of inorganic chemistry, carbon is a unique element due to its ability to form an immense number of distinct compounds. Current estimates suggest that nearly ten million carbon-containing compounds are known, though the actual number may be even greater. Organic Compounds Every organic compound contains at least one carbon atom. The number of organic compounds is vast, with approximately ten million defined compounds identified. However, the theoretical number of possible organic compounds is much larger. Some compounds, such as ammonium carbamate (NH₂COONH₄), phosgene (COCl₂), thiophosgene (CSCl₂), thiourea (CS(NH₂)₂), and urea (CO(NH₂)₂), are sometimes classified as inorganic despite containing carbon. Inorganic Compounds Inorganic carbon chemistry encompasses a wide variety of compounds that do not fall under the domain of organic chemistry. Compounds with Other Nonmetals The most well-known inorganic carbon compounds are the oxides of carbon, including carbon dioxide (CO₂) and carbon monoxide (CO). Other less common oxides include carbon suboxide (C₃O₂), dicarbon monoxide (C₂O), and the exotic carbon trioxide (CO₃). Binary compounds of carbon with nonmetals include carbon disulfide (CS₂), beta-carbon nitride (β-C₃N₄), carbon tetrabromide (CBr₄), carbon tetrachloride (CCl₄), carbon tetrafluoride (CF₄), carbonyl fluoride (COF₂), carbonyl sulfide (COS), and dicarbaborane (H₂C₂B₁₀H₁₀). Compounds with Metals The only known acid derived from carbon oxides is carbonic acid (H₂CO₃). Upon losing a proton, it forms bicarbonates, which can further deprotonate to form carbonates. Examples of bicarbonates and carbonates include ammonium bicarbonate (NH₄HCO₃), ammonium carbonate ((NH₄)₂CO₃), barium carbonate (BaCO₃), calcium carbonate (CaCO₃), and sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃), among others. Metal carbonyls are coordination complexes formed between transition metals and carbonyl ligands (CO). These complexes are covalent in nature. Examples include chromium hexacarbonyl (Cr(CO)₆), cobalt octacarbonyl (Co₂(CO)₈), iron pentacarbonyl (Fe(CO)₅), and nickel tetracarbonyl (Ni(CO)₄). Other inorganic compounds include salts and complexes of carbon-containing polyatomic ions such as cyanide (CN⁻), isocyanide (NC⁻), cyanate (OCN⁻), and thiocyanate (SCN⁻). Examples include potassium cyanide (KCN), sodium thiocyanate (NaSCN), and ferricyanide (K₃Fe(CN)₆). Carbides Carbides are binary compounds of carbon with elements that are less electronegative than carbon. Examples include boron carbide (B₄C), calcium carbide (CaC₂), silicon carbide (SiC), tantalum carbide (TaC), titanium carbide (TiC), and tungsten carbide (WC). The study of carbon allotropes, such as diamond, graphite, and fullerenes, has expanded significantly since the discovery of buckminsterfullerene (C₆₀) in 1985. Fullerenes and their derivatives, including inclusion compounds where ions are encapsulated within the carbon shell, represent a fascinating area of research. For instance, a lithium ion trapped within a buckminsterfullerene molecule is denoted as Li⁺@C₆₀. These complex ions can pair with counterions to form salts. Alloys Several alloys contain carbon, with carbon steel being the most well-known. Other iron-carbon alloys include anthracite iron, cast iron, pig iron, wrought iron, and spiegel iron (which also contains manganese). Stellite, an alloy of carbon with cobalt, chromium, and tungsten, is another example. These alloys can, to some extent, be considered carbides. Formation of Carbon Compounds In organic chemistry, carbon, oxygen, and hydrogen are the three most important elements. Each of these elements forms bonds with specific valencies: carbon forms tetravalent bonds, oxygen forms divalent bonds, and hydrogen forms monovalent bonds. This bonding versatility underpins the vast diversity of carbon compounds.
